title: Target Decoy FDR
text:
Types of FDR
We define
 * false positives (FP) as the number of passing decoy assignments
 * true positives (TP) as the number of passing forward hits.

FDR of a concatenated target-decoy search
Which is the “Fraction of incorrect assignments above score threshold”. The multiplier 2 is needed here since we assume that also the forward sequences have false assignments.
\[
FDR_{concatenated} = \frac{2 \cdot FP}{TP + FP}
\]
This is taken from the reference by (Elias and Gygi 2007). It is often called the false positive rate (FPR), which (Storey and Tibshirani 2003) defines differently. Kaell points out that this quantity actually should be named FDR and that “Many proteomics papers incorrectly refer to this quantity as the false positive rate.” TargetDecoyFDR therefore names it fdr_concatenated.


Simple FDR
“The FDR associated with a particular score threshold is defined as the expected percentage of accepted PSMs that are incorrect, where an accepted PSM is one that scores above the threshold (Many proteomics papers incorrectly refer to this quantity as the false positive rate).” ((Käll et al. 2007))
The Simple FDR introduced by ((Käll et al. 2007)) is defined by :
\[
SimpleFDR =  \frac{FP}{TP}
\]
“For a given score threshold, we count the number of decoy PSMs above the threshold and the number of target PSMs above the threshold. We can now estimate the FDR by simply computing the ratio of these two values (SimpleFDR).”(Käll et al. 2007)

fdr_curves <- data.frame(
  score = rep(fdr1$table$score, 2),
  fdr = 100 * c(fdr1$table$simple_fdr, fdr1$table$q_value_simple_fdr),
  curve = rep(c("SimpleFDR", "q-value"), each = fdr1$n)
)
ggplot(fdr_curves, aes(x = score, y = fdr, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.002), ylim = c(0, 0.05)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(SimpleFDR = "black", "q-value" = "#E69F00")) +
  labs(x = "score (smaller is better)", y = "FDR (%)", colour = NULL)








Although the score is getting better (smaller) the FDR may increase since the number of TP in the denominator decreases while the number of FP stays the same. Therefore Storey and Tibshirani proposed the q-value, “which in our case is defined as the minimal FDR threshold at which a given PSM is accepted”(Käll et al. 2007).

section: Creating a FASTA database from the command line
text:
Creating a FASTA database from the command line
prozor installs the script fgcz_create_fasta.R (it needs the docopt package). It reads all FASTA files and the annotation.txt in a directory, adds contaminants and reversed decoy sequences, and writes one FASTA file:
script=$(Rscript -e 'cat(system.file("script", "fgcz_create_fasta.R", package = "prozor"))')
Rscript "$script" -h
Rscript "$script" path/to/database_dir -o path/to/output_dir
Rscript "$script" path/to/database_dir nodecoy -c none -o path/to/output_dir

Result columns and list elements are snake_case too:

annotate_aho(), annotate_peptides(): protein_id, offset, protein_sequence, peptide_length, and peptide_seq for vector input (was proteinID, Offset, proteinSequence, lengthPeptide, peptideSeq)
greedy_to_table(): peptide, precursor_charge, protein (was Peptide, precursorCharge, Protein); precursor_charge is an integer instead of a character
make_fasta_summary(as_string = FALSE): nr_sequences, length_summary, aa_freq; create_fgcz_fasta_db(): db, file_path, summary, call, db_name

The target-decoy FDR functions computeFDR(), computeFDRwithID(), predictScoreFDR() and plotFDR() are replaced by the R6 class TargetDecoyFDR, without aliases. TargetDecoyFDR$new(score, decoy_hit, larger_better = TRUE, id = NULL) sorts the hits and computes both FDR estimates and their q-values once; the read-only fields larger_better, n (number of hits) and table hold the result. table is a data frame in the sorted order with the columns order, id (only when given), score, decoy_hit, fdr_concatenated, simple_fdr, q_value_fdr_concatenated and q_value_simple_fdr; computeFDR() returned a list of vectors with FPR, SimpleFDR, qValue_FPR, qValue_SimpleFDR and, from computeFDRwithID(), ID. FPR became fdr_concatenated because 2 * decoys / all hits estimates the FDR of a concatenated target-decoy search, not a false positive rate. $score_at(q_value = 0.01, method = c("simple_fdr", "fdr_concatenated")) replaces predictScoreFDR(): method takes "simple_fdr" (default) or "fdr_concatenated" (was "SimpleFDR", "FPR"), and q_value is a fraction like the q-values in table, 0.01 for 1 % (the default); qValue was in percent, and values outside 0 to 1 stop with an error. $plot() replaces plotFDR(), with the new names in its legend, and print() shows the numbers of hits and decoys and the scores at simple_fdr q-values of 0.01 and 0.05. The decoys are given as flags only: for protein IDs, pass decoy_hit = grepl("^REV_", id), id = id, which counts only IDs starting with REV_ as decoys; computeFDRwithID() matched its default decoy = "REV_" anywhere in the ID.
Default column names follow the results: annotate_peptides(peptide = "peptide_seq"), and greedy_parsimony(peptide = "peptide_seq") reads the proteins from protein_id (was annotatePeptides(peptide = "peptideSeq") and prepareMatrix(proteinID = "proteinID", peptideID = "strippedSequence")).
The data sets fdr_sample, protpepmetashort and pepprot have snake_case columns (protein_id, peptide_seq, peptide_mod_seq, precursor_charge, protein_length, peptide_length); bcd keeps COMET’s column names.
greedy(), last on CRAN in 0.3.1, has no alias; use greedy_parsimony(annotation, peptide = "peptide_seq"). It takes the peptide-protein matches as a data frame, e.g. the result of annotate_peptides(), instead of a peptide-by-protein matrix: the protein IDs in the column protein_id and the peptide IDs in the column named by peptide (for precursors, add a column such as paste(peptide_seq, precursor_charge, sep = ".")). A peptide-protein pair in several rows counts once, and ties go to the protein first in factor(protein_id), as with prepareMatrix(). It stops for missing columns, naming them, and for NA IDs, counting them. annotate_peptides() and greedy_parsimony() accept tibbles; a tibble passed to annotatePeptides() or prepareMatrix() used to crash R or fail with “cannot xtfrm data frames”.
write_fasta() keeps a > inside a header (ADP>ATP used to become ADPATP).
remove_signal_peptide() reads UniProt’s current signal peptide format SIGNAL 1..20, and works on a database with a single entry.
remove_signal_peptide() stops when a name of db has no | and so no UniProt accession, or signal$Entry is NA; such entries skipped the check that signal lists the entries in the order of db.
remove_signal_peptide() gives a shortened sequence its new ID as list name too, so annotate_aho() and the written FASTA file report the same ID, and keeps the description in its header (it used to keep the old ID as list name and drop the description).
Cdsw$new(method = "sampling") stops with an error when even equal-width windows violate minwindow or maxwindow; sampling_breaks() used to warn and then never return.
Constant breaks enclose the masses for any digits, and readjust_windows() and Cdsw$optimize_windows() work for any bin width. The mass range was rounded to 2 decimals in constant_breaks() and to 1 in readjust_windows(), whatever digits was, so the outer breaks could lie inside the range of the masses: constant_breaks(digits = 3) followed by $plot() or $error(), and readjust_windows(digits = 2), failed with “some ‘x’ not counted; maybe ‘breaks’ do not span range of ‘x’” for about 38 % of data sets. The range is now rounded outward to multiples of 1 / 10^digits (of bin_width in readjust_windows()) and padded by one such unit. With the default digits the breaks are the same; other values give slightly different breaks (on masses, by at most one unit of the last digit for digits 0 and 1, and 0.004 m/z for 3 and 4), and the bins of readjust_windows(bin_width = 1) start at whole m/z values.
readjust_windows() and Cdsw$optimize_windows() also move a window start down to the first empty bin and a window end up to the last one; such boundaries stayed in place when that bin was the nearest. On masses, the first window of optimize_windows(maxbin = 10) starts at 350.05 instead of 350.13. When no bin is empty, e.g. with maxbin = 0, the windows are returned unchanged; this failed with “argument is of length zero”.
The breaks of Cdsw are unnamed for all methods, so Cdsw$as_table() has row numbers instead of the quantile names 0%, 4%, …, which did not describe mixed breaks.
annotate_peptides() removes whitespace around the peptides, e.g. the "\r" of a file with Windows line endings, before it counts, searches and merges them. Such peptides were found but then dropped from the result without a warning; when all peptides had whitespace, the result was an empty data frame.
annotate_aho() and annotate_peptides() search proteins with lower-case residues or characters other than letters, such as the stop codon * of translated databases: the sequences are searched in upper case, with X for each other character, so the offsets stay the same. One such protein used to stop the whole search with “character ’*’ is not in the trie’s alphabet”.
The help of annotate_peptides() says what matched checks: by default, that the peptide is preceded by K or R or the protein N-terminus (or by the Met at position 1). The end of the peptide is not checked.
annotate_aho() is faster: 0.02 s instead of 0.12 s for the 1,520 bundled peptides against 1,072 proteins.
annotate_aho() and annotate_peptides() no longer print dplyr’s “Joining with by = join_by(proteinID)” message, nor dplyr’s funs() deprecation warning.
Error messages name the argument and the offending value, e.g. for an unknown method of TargetDecoyFDR$score_at().
greedy_parsimony() ignores unused factor levels of the ID columns, so it works on subsets of the bundled data sets. prepareMatrix() failed on them with “length of Dimnames[[2]] (250) is not equal to Dim[2] (239)”, or gave a peptide row or protein column without entries.
write_fasta(), make_fasta_summary() and reverse_seq() are faster and give the same output: for 82,000 proteins and their decoys, writing takes 0.9 s instead of 11 s, the summary 0.6 s instead of 10 s and the reversal 1.2 s instead of 3.8 s, and create_fgcz_fasta_db() 4.7 s instead of 30 s.
read_peptide_fasta() gives an entry without sequence lines (a header followed directly by the next header, or a header on the last line) the empty string. It used to return the next header pasted to this one, e.g. ">b>a", or "NA>b" for the last entry, which write_fasta() then wrote as an extra header line.
make_fasta_summary() gives an empty sequence the length 0 in the length summary (it counted 1).
load_contaminants("special2024") works: the bundled fgcz_special_prot_20241112.fasta.gz is a plain gzipped FASTA file again instead of a gzipped tar archive (#7).
create_fgcz_fasta_db() reads only FASTA files (*.fasta, *.fa or *.faa, optionally gzipped) and the file annotation.txt, and stops when database_dir holds no FASTA file or when output_dir is database_dir. It used to read every file with fasta in its name: a *.fa.gz database was skipped and the output held only the contaminants, and a second run read the database written into database_dir as targets, so target sequences were labeled as decoys (REV_REV_).
create_decoy_db() keeps only the first entry of each name, as create_fgcz_fasta_db() did. It used to return duplicated names, e.g. 1010 when a target file holds the default contaminants, and annotate_aho() refused the result.
load_contaminants(no_human = TRUE) also drops entries whose header says Homo sapiens; it kept 7 human keratins of the "fgcz2019", "fgcz2021" and "fgcz2022" sets.
inst/script/fgcz_create_fasta.R --contamin takes every set of load_contaminants(), also universal2024 and special2024, besides special, none and a FASTA file, and stops early naming the sets for an unknown value. The parameter log of a nodecoy run says revLab: NULL instead of REV_.
The summary of create_fgcz_fasta_db() and the parameter log of fgcz_create_fasta.R record the argument values, e.g. contaminants : 505 sequences, instead of the call, which showed contaminants = contaminants when run from the script. The summary no longer contains a link to the FGCZ intranet.
The dummy entry CRAPCRAPCRAP that create_decoy_db() puts first has the attributes it gets when the written file is read back: Annot starts with > and name is the first word of the header (it was the whole annotation line). The written files are unchanged.
The FGCZ shell wrappers (inst/script/*.sh) and the notes in inst/creatingDBs/ are no longer part of the package; inst/script/fgcz_create_fasta.R stays.
load_contaminants() cites the source of the "universal2024" set; inst/COPYRIGHTS lists its origin.
Help pages use markdown, link related functions in families, and describe the actual return values (e.g. the columns of TargetDecoyFDR$table).
?create_fgcz_fasta_db gives the memory a build needs (about 4 KB per written sequence), and ?greedy_parsimony says that protein groups are formed on the peptides left in each round. pepprot is titled “Precursors of identified peptides”, as it holds no proteins.
New or runnable examples for create_fgcz_fasta_db(), greedy_to_table(), remove_signal_peptide() and write_fasta(); removed debugging code from examples and vignettes.
The vignettes use the new names and ggplot2; “Peptide Annotation and Protein Inference” builds again. “Creating Target Decoy Databases” finds the FASTA files as create_fgcz_fasta_db() does, writes to tempdir() and ends with the one-call create_fgcz_fasta_db().
The Cdsw help page documents each method with its usage and arguments; it documented method arguments without a usage section (r-devel NOTE).
Removed the undocumented debug data set mm.
Fewer dependencies: Matrix, protViz, purrr, rlang and seqinr are no longer needed, so a default install also skips the five packages only seqinr needed, RcppArmadillo among them; dplyr and docopt moved to Suggests (dplyr is only used by the vignettes and tests, docopt only by inst/script/fgcz_create_fasta.R).

title: prozor
text:
Reads one or more FASTA files, adds contaminants and reversed decoy sequences, and puts first a dummy entry CRAPCRAPCRAP whose header records the source of the database. Of entries with the same name, only the first is kept. See vignette(“CreatingDecoyDB”, package = “prozor”).



create_decoy_db(
  dbs,
  contaminants = c(load_contaminants("special2024"), load_contaminants("universal2024")),
  rev_lab = "REV_",
  annot = "zz|sourceOf|database"
)







dbs


Paths to one or more FASTA files.




contaminants


A list of contaminant sequences, e.g. from load_contaminants(), or NULL for none.




rev_lab


Prefix of the reversed decoy sequences, or NULL for no decoys.




annot


Header of the dummy entry that records the source of the database, with or without the leading >.






A list of SeqFastaAA objects with unique names: the dummy entry, the targets, the contaminants and, unless rev_lab is NULL, the reversed decoys of the targets and contaminants.



Other FASTA databases: create_fgcz_fasta_db(), load_contaminants(), make_chain_id(), make_chain_id_uniprot(), make_fasta_summary(), read_peptide_fasta(), remove_signal_peptide(), reverse_seq(), write_fasta()




library("prozor")

file <- system.file("extdata/fgcz_contaminants2022_20220405.fasta.gz", package = "prozor")
targets <- read_peptide_fasta(file)
cont <- load_contaminants("fgcz2022")

# the file, read twice, holds the same entries as the default contaminants: each is kept once
db <- create_decoy_db(c(file, file), contaminants = cont)
stopifnot(length(db) == 1 + 2 * length(targets), identical(names(targets), names(cont)))

db <- create_decoy_db(file, rev_lab = NULL, contaminants = NULL)
stopifnot(length(db) == 1 + length(targets))

text:
Repeatedly assigns all unexplained peptides of the protein that explains the most of them. Proteins that explain exactly the same unexplained peptides are reported together, separated by ;. The groups are formed on the peptides that remain in each round: proteins B (peptides p1, p5, p6) and C (p2, p5, p6) form the group “B;C” for p5 and p6 after protein A has taken p1 and p2.



greedy_parsimony(annotation, peptide = "peptide_seq")







annotation


A data frame (or tibble) with one row per peptide-protein match, e.g. from annotate_peptides(): the protein IDs in the column protein_id and the peptide IDs in the column named by peptide (character or factor columns, without NA; unused factor levels are ignored).




peptide


Name of the column with the peptide IDs. For precursors, add a column such as paste(peptide_seq, precursor_charge, sep = “.”) and pass its name.






Proteins are ranked by the number of distinct peptides they explain; a peptide-protein pair that occurs in several rows counts once. Of the proteins that tie, the one first in factor(annotation$protein_id) is taken first: alphabetical order for a character column, the level order for a factor column.



A named list with one element per distinct peptide ID: the protein, or ;-separated protein group, it is assigned to. The elements are in the order in which the groups are chosen, and the peptides of a group in the order of factor(annotation[[peptide]]).

# every modified peptide is assigned to exactly one protein group

text:
An R6 class that splits the MS1 mass range into nbins windows with about equal numbers of precursors. The window boundaries (breaks) are computed once, when the object is created, with one of three methods:


“sampling” (default): the quantile breaks of the masses mixed with uniformly spread data, with the smallest share of uniform data that keeps all window widths within [minwindow, maxwindow]; the quantile breaks themselves if they fit. Stops if even windows of equal width violate the limits.


“quantile”: windows with equal numbers of masses, of any width.


“constant”: windows of equal width.


The breaks are rounded to digits decimals, and the outer breaks are rounded outward and padded by 1 / 10^digits, so that the windows enclose all masses.
The object cannot be changed: its fields are read-only and its methods only read them, so their results do not depend on the order in which they are called. To compare methods or settings, create one object for each. clone() copies an object.






masses


MS1 masses (read-only).


nbins


Number of windows (read-only).


method


Method that placed the breaks (read-only).


breaks


Window boundaries, nbins + 1 values (read-only).

  masses,
  nbins = 25,
  method = c("sampling", "quantile", "constant"),
  maxwindow = 150,
  minwindow = 5,
  digits = 2
)





masses


MS1 masses (m/z): a numeric vector of finite values.


nbins


Number of windows.


method


How to place the breaks: “sampling” (default), “quantile” or “constant”; see Description.


maxwindow, minwindow


Largest and smallest window width in m/z; used by method = “sampling” only.


digits


Number of decimal places of the breaks.

…

Overlap of neighboring windows in m/z: each window is widened by overlap / 2 on both sides.




A data frame with one row per window: start from, end to, center mid, width and the number of precursors with from < m/z <= to (counts).



Deviation of the windows from equal numbers of precursors.


Cdsw\$error()


A list with score1 (Manhattan distance), score2 (Euclidean distance), counts (precursors per window) and optimum_n (equal counts), both counts normalized to length 1.



Move window starts and ends to regions with few precursors, with readjust_windows().


Cdsw\$optimize_windows(bin_width = 0.1, maxbin = 15, overlap = 0)

Width of the bins (m/z) into which the masses are binned.

A data frame with the columns of as_table().

Plot the DIA cycle, one window per step.

A ggplot object.

  database_dir,
  contaminants = c(load_contaminants("special2024"), load_contaminants("universal2024")),

  output_dir,

)







database_dir


Directory with the FASTA files and annotation.txt.




contaminants


Contaminant sequences to add, e.g. from load_contaminants(), or NULL for none.




rev_lab


Prefix of the reversed decoy sequences, or NULL for no decoys.




output_dir


Directory the FASTA file is written to; must not be database_dir, where the next run would read the written database as targets.




make_summary


If TRUE, append the output of make_fasta_summary() to the summary.

title: prozor
text:
An R6 class that estimates the false discovery rate (FDR) of target-decoy search results. When the object is created, the hits are sorted from best to worst score and two FDR estimates are computed at each score:


fdr_concatenated: the FDR of a concatenated target-decoy search, estimated as 2 * decoys / all hits (Elias and Gygi).


simple_fdr: the FDR estimated as decoys / targets (Kaell).


The q-value of a hit is the lowest FDR at which it is accepted: the smallest estimate at its own or any worse score. Within tied scores, decoys are ranked before targets, so the result does not depend on the input order and tied targets get the conservative FDR.
The decoys are given as logical flags. For protein IDs whose decoys start with REV_, pass decoy_hit = grepl(“^REV_”, id), and id = id to keep the IDs in table.
The object cannot be changed: its fields are read-only and its methods only read them. clone() copies an object. See vignette(“TargetDecoyFDR_Example”, package = “prozor”).






larger_better


TRUE if a larger score is better (read-only).


n


Number of hits (read-only).


table


The hits from best to worst score, as a data frame (read-only) with the columns:


order: the position of the hit in the input.


id: the ID of the hit; only when id was given.


score, decoy_hit: the sorted input.


fdr_concatenated, simple_fdr: the FDR estimates at the score.


q_value_fdr_concatenated, q_value_simple_fdr: the q-values of both estimates, as fractions.

Search engine scores, without NA.


decoy_hit


Logical, TRUE for decoy hits, one per score, without NA.


larger_better


TRUE if a larger score is better, FALSE if a smaller score is better.


id


IDs of the hits, e.g. protein IDs, one per score; NULL (default) for none.




A new TargetDecoyFDR object.



Print the numbers of hits and decoys, larger_better, and the scores at simple_fdr q-values of 0.01 and 0.05 (none if no score reaches them).

The object, invisibly.



Find the score cut-off for a given FDR.

  q_value = 0.01,

method


The FDR estimate to use: “simple_fdr” (default) or “fdr_concatenated”.




The least strict score whose q-value is at most q_value. An error if no score reaches it.

Finds every occurrence of each peptide in fasta with annotate_aho() and flags whether it is preceded by a tryptic cleavage site. Peptides that occur in no protein are dropped.



annotate_peptides(
  pepinfo,
  fasta,
  peptide = "peptide_seq",
  prefix = "(([RK])|(^)|(^M))",
  suffix = ""
)







pepinfo


A character vector of peptide sequences, or a data frame (or tibble) with the column peptide and any further columns, such as the charge state, which are kept. It must not have the columns protein_id, offset, protein_sequence, matched or peptide_length, which the result adds.




fasta


A list of protein sequences with unique names, as returned by read_peptide_fasta().




peptide


Name of the column with the peptide sequences.




prefix


Regular expression the residues before a match must end with.




suffix


Regular expression the residues after a match must start with.






Each occurrence of a peptide in a protein is one row. matched is TRUE when the residues before that occurrence match prefix and the residues after it match suffix. With the defaults, matched means: preceded by K or R or the protein N-terminus (or by the Met at position 1). Whitespace around the peptide sequences, such as the “ of a file with Windows line endings, is removed before the search, and the result holds the trimmed sequences.

title: Protein Sequence Coverage
text:
library(prozor)
library(ggplot2)


Introduction
The sequence coverage of a protein is the fraction of its residues that the identified peptides cover. It tells how much of a protein the data actually support: a protein identified by one short peptide is weaker evidence than one whose sequence is covered from end to end. Per residue, coverage shows which regions the peptides support, and, for proteins with several isoforms, whether the peptides cover the stretches that tell the isoforms apart.
prozor computes coverage from the result of annotate_peptides() (or annotate_aho()):

residue_coverage() counts, for every residue, how many distinct peptides cover it;
sequence_coverage() summarizes this per protein;
plot_coverage() draws a protein sequence with each residue colored by its coverage.



Data
The example data are the peptides identified in a human sample (IDResults.txt.gz) and two FASTA databases: one with canonical sequences only and one that also contains isoforms.

file <- system.file("extdata/IDResults.txt.gz", package = "prozor")
peptides <- unique(utils::read.delim(file)$peptideSeq)
canonical <- read_peptide_fasta(system.file("p1000_db1_example/Annotation_canSeq.fasta.gz", package = "prozor"))
all_sequences <- read_peptide_fasta(system.file("p1000_db1_example/Annotation_allSeq.fasta.gz", package = "prozor"))
c(peptides = length(peptides), canonical = length(canonical), with_isoforms = length(all_sequences))

     peptides     canonical with_isoforms 
         1520           382          1072 




Coverage per protein
First we find the proteins each peptide occurs in, then summarize the coverage per protein.

annotation <- annotate_peptides(peptides, canonical)
coverage <- sequence_coverage(annotation)
head(coverage)

greedy_parsimony() keeps the smallest set of proteins that explains all peptides (see vignette("PeptideAnnotationwithProzor", package = "prozor")). The proteins it drops are those whose peptides are all explained by other proteins; they tend to have lower coverage.

Isoforms
With isoforms in the database, a peptide can match several sequences of the same gene. Coverage along the sequences shows which parts of each isoform the peptides support. Kininogen-1 (KNG1, UniProt P01042) is an example: its high-molecular-weight form (the canonical sequence) and its low-molecular-weight form (isoform 2) share the N-terminal part and differ in the C-terminal part.

annotation_all <- annotate_peptides(peptides, all_sequences)

isoform_counts <- c(
  shared = length(intersect(kng1_peptides[[1]], kng1_peptides[[2]])),
  canonical_only = length(setdiff(kng1_peptides[[1]], kng1_peptides[[2]])),
  isoform_2_only = length(setdiff(kng1_peptides[[2]], kng1_peptides[[1]]))
)

Isoform 2 has the higher coverage only because it is shorter: the 18 shared peptides cover the common N-terminal part of both sequences. The C-terminal part of isoform 2 is not covered. The isoform-specific evidence is the 1 peptide(s) in the C-terminal part of the canonical sequence, which isoform 2 lacks: only they show that the high-molecular-weight form is present. Judged by coverage fraction alone, isoform 2 would look like the better-supported form.
